stories.headline: Gunmen Kill at Least 10 Villagers, Loot Shops in Northeast Nigeria
stories.summary:
Unknown gunmen raided the remote village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area of Taraba state, northeastern Nigeria, on Friday, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police said. The attackers reportedly arrived on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers, and the rampage is said to have lasted up to four hours.

Police recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after responding to a distress call, but the attackers had fled by the time officers arrived. Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said officers were searching the nearby bush for other casualties and warned the toll could rise. Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told AFP the attackers came on about 50 motorcycles, two men to each, and took cash, food and abandoned motorcycles. Survivors counted at least 20 dead, and some residents remain missing.

Amnesty International's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, said families of the bereaved told the group up to 50 people died, noting that the initial funeral had 37 people. He called for an impartial investigation and accused authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity."

The attack adds to a pattern of violence by armed groups across Nigeria's northwest, northeast and central regions. The country is also fighting a jihadist insurgency in the northeast that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of security.

stories.headline: Higher Energy Costs Weigh on Trump's Midterm Pitch as Obama Rallies in Michigan
stories.summary:
With the November 3 midterms about a week away, the Iran war and higher energy prices are shaping voters' economic concerns, according to analysis aired on Bloomberg. Financial Times associate editor Rana Foroohar said rising costs are a central factor as both parties push into the final stretch of early voting.

Former President Barack Obama rallied in Detroit on Saturday, the first day of early voting in Michigan, for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He blamed inflation and high prices on President Trump, called him an agent of "chaos and cruelty," and warned of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values. The race could hinge on Detroit's substantial Black vote, and some undecided Black voters told reporters the endorsement had not swayed them. Republican candidate Mike Rogers, responding to Trump's description of El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and "violent terrorist," gave an interview to Meet the Press.

Trump defended his tariff policy at a Georgia rally, saying it has made the country richer, and announced that Volkswagen would build a $4.2 billion Audi plant in the state. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt described a strategy to rally Trump supporters who typically skip midterm elections and to counter weak approval ratings. A Federal Reserve report also found median family net worth rose from 2022 to 2025 for all racial and ethnic groups except Black families, whose median net worth fell 25%.

stories.headline: El Salvador's Bukele Says Bodies Handed Over in Haiti Are Not Missing Hostages
stories.summary:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said four bodies delivered to his country's special forces in Haiti are "not our men," casting doubt on whether the four missing Salvadoran air technicians have been found. He said a nongovernmental organization handed over the remains at a Haitian airport, claiming they were the missing men, but that one body was a child's and another wore a uniform from a different country's army.

Bukele posted images of a Gang Suppression Force member's ID card and a matching Chad national ID. His account contradicts a New York Times report, citing people close to the mission, that the badly burned bodies found near Port-au-Prince on Saturday were believed to be the missing men. One unnamed source told the paper the ID Bukele posted belonged to a soldier who lost it when he was injured.

The four men were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force and vanished after an ambush by heavily armed criminal groups in the Croix-des-Bouquets area. Bukele dispatched a military contingent on Thursday, reportedly about 450 soldiers, with the stated aim of returning the men alive.

Haiti has been consumed by gang violence since the 2021 assassination of its president, and the UN reported more than 5,700 people killed or injured between January 1 and September 11. The multinational force has struggled to enter areas gangs control. Identification of the remains is expected to require medical examination.

stories.headline: Trump's Former Border Patrol Chief Calls Minneapolis Withdrawal a 'Surrender'
stories.summary:
Greg Bovino, the former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the Minneapolis deportation drive, told the BBC the administration's withdrawal of agents from the city was a "surrender." Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, he said the administration "threw the towel in," that deportations were at a "virtual standstill," and that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota."

Bovino was removed from his role after the January shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti, which were captured on video and prompted a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he would "de-escalate a little bit" and pulled about 700 immigration agents from the state. Earlier this month Good's family filed two civil lawsuits alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with protesters' civil rights, naming Bovino and agent Jonathan Ross, who shot Good.

Bovino said he was "not responding" to the suit and that "people do lawsuits all the time." He rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined claims that Good and Pretti meant to harm agents, calling his agents the "real victims." The family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and said they look forward to deposing him. The White House has called the lawsuits "baseless."

stories.headline: Update: Israel Imposes West Bank Movement Restrictions Ahead of Pivotal Tuesday Election as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Escalate
stories.summary:
The Israeli military announced restrictions on the movement of Palestinian workers in the run-up to Tuesday's national election. The measures follow the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen on Friday near Hebron, which prompted a full lockdown of the West Bank. Many Israelis view the vote as one of the most pivotal in the country's history, with implications beyond its borders.

Campaign coverage has focused on the ultra-Orthodox community's resistance to military conscription and whether it could bring down the Netanyahu government. Arab Israeli turnout, often depressed by disaffection, is the subject of a strong push to remove the right-wing governing coalition. More than half a million young people are also expected to vote for the first time, and could prove decisive. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to take personal responsibility for the failures surrounding the October 2023 attack or to order a state inquiry.

Elsewhere in the region, the Iran-backed Houthi movement has continued strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities, with at least three deaths reported in the latest attacks at an airport and an oil field. The United Kingdom said it will provide additional defensive military support to Saudi Arabia. Yemen's army said three missiles hit a training camp in government-controlled Shabwa province on Monday.

Warnings to US officials have also intensified. The State Department has adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, and a separate attack in Jordan's southern Karak governorate left 34 people injured, with a manhunt under way.

stories.headline: Update: Almost 1,000 Arrested in French Protests as Clashes Erupt After Largely Peaceful Marches
stories.summary:
French police fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse protesters after clashes broke out following a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations across the country. Officials said almost 1,000 people were arrested, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Authorities estimated about 410,000 people took part, while unions put the figure at roughly 800,000.

In Paris, objects were thrown at police and the demonstration turned violent. In Marseille, protesters set barricades and rubbish bins alight, and in Bordeaux demonstrators ripped boards from a shop to build a barricade. In Grenoble, hundreds of masked individuals vandalized property and attacked police with mortars and projectiles, according to officials.

Authorities appear to have avoided a repeat of the rioting and looting of 17 October, which produced some of the worst disorder in modern French history and led to more than 2,700 arrests. The government had deployed tens of thousands of officers and closed the Louvre in anticipation of unrest. President Emmanuel Macron has pledged to overhaul university admissions after meeting protesting students, though the movement has continued.

stories.headline: Update: Serbia Votes in Watershed Election as Student-Led List Challenges Vučić
stories.summary:
Serbians went to the polls in a parliamentary election that will decide whether longtime strongman Aleksandar Vučić returns as prime minister or is ousted by an unprecedented student-led opposition. The students campaign on cracking down on corruption and strengthening democracy.

The vote is widely seen as a test of Vučić's grip on power after a prolonged period of student-driven protest. Analysts describe the race as tight, with the student list the most serious challenge his camp has faced in years.

Results and any disputes over the conduct of the vote will determine whether Serbia's government changes hands or Vučić consolidates his position.

stories.headline: Twelve Injured, Including Six Children, in Shooting Near Florida A&M Stadium During Homecoming Week
stories.summary:
A shooting near Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium in Tallahassee on Saturday night left 12 people injured, including six juveniles, police said. The shooting occurred just before 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets. Eleven victims sustained gunshot wounds, and the youngest victim was 11.

One victim was in critical condition, two were seriously injured and eight were stable. Police Chief Lawrence Revell said preliminary information indicated a physical altercation involving two or three individuals preceded the gunfire, and described it as an isolated incident. No arrests had been announced.

The shooting took place during the university's Homecoming Week, when students and alumni gather for annual celebrations. Revell said officers carried victims to safety and transported them to hospitals before the scene was fully secure. The university said the campus remained safe and urged people to avoid the area while the investigation continued.
